source.title: Batch Size Matters: A Diffusion Approximation Framework on Nonconvex Stochastic Gradient Descent
source.authors: C. Li; Lei Li; Jun-Yang Qian; Jian-Guo Liu

record.file_problem: Full paper text supplied. The conclusion heading is incomplete (“Section ??”), but the relevant sections and numerical experiment are present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper tests batch-size effects on train/test accuracy in an MNIST network, using the same accuracy-gap outcome but a different study and experiment from the cited large-batch work.
record.gate_note: Section 5’s diffusion analysis and claims about sharp or flat minima are theoretical interpretation, not separate measured results for the mapped versions. The numerical experiment reports the train/test accuracy gap across batch sizes in Figures 3–4; exact plotted values are figure-only. Figures 1–2 measure weight distance, and Figures 5–6 report test accuracy during continued training from selected initial weights; these do not separately measure the version’s fixed-epoch train/test gap.
record.test_reason: The study reports its own batch-size experiments, but Figures 3–4 hold optimizer iterations fixed, whereas V5 specifies fixed epochs. Larger batches therefore process more examples. The reported widening train–test gap does not establish V5's fixed-epoch held-out performance penalty. The diffusion theory does not test V7's magnitude-aware sharpness measure.
record.authors_conclusion: The record correctly summarizes the proposed benefit of small batches for escaping stationary points and increasing batch size later for settling. It incorrectly says the text gives no direction for the accuracy results: Section 6 explicitly reports a wider train–test gap with larger batches and particularly low test accuracy despite high training accuracy for large batches. The increasing-batch schedule is a theoretical recommendation, not an experimentally demonstrated recovery.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies SGD batch size and the train/test accuracy gap in a fully connected MNIST model, but does not report the exact plotted accuracy values in text. Its central contribution is a diffusion-approximation framework for nonconvex SGD.
record.method_sensitivity: Batch size; training duration; initialization from the best small-batch or large-batch weights; momentum setting in the experiment.

fits_no_version.finding: Section 6 explicitly reports a widening train–test accuracy gap with increasing batch size. Figures 3–4 compare equal iterations at learning rate 0.1, with momentum 0 and 0.9, respectively; numerical accuracies are unavailable in the supplied text.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Larger batches can produce a wider train–test accuracy gap in a batch-normalized fully connected MNIST network under equal optimizer-update budgets.

fits_no_version.finding: Figures 5–6 restart training from selected best small-batch or large-batch weights. The narrative describes large-batch settling in relatively flat regions and small-batch escape from relatively sharp regions, without recoverable numerical comparisons.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The benefit of batch size during continued training can depend on the starting weights and training duration.

record.problems: The batch-size accuracy results are shown only in Figures 3–4, with no exact values or written description of the plotted direction. The text says the experiments use the same number of iterations, while V5 specifies a fixed epoch budget. The plotted values cannot be assigned precisely from the supplied text.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted. The batch-size train/test accuracy plots are relevant but cannot be recorded as result rows because the text provides no exact values and no verbal description of their direction; Figures 3–4 are figure-only.

untested.parts: Test error as width increases beyond zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under specified tuning.
Held-out performance across batch sizes with epochs held fixed; recovery of that penalty through longer training or recipe changes.
Magnitude-aware sharpness versus generalization gaps and competing predictors.
Removing memorized examples versus removing random examples.

record.verdict_notes: There are no extracted rows to fix. The accuracy plots are already declared in rows_left_out, so they are not additional missing results. Exact numerical values are unnecessary to record an explicit qualitative result, but the equal-iteration design prevents a verdict on V5's fixed-epoch claim.

versions.untested_parts: The paper does not compare fitting random labels with generalization on natural labels.
No network-width sweep or interpolation-threshold analysis.
No convolutional versus fully connected architecture comparison.

The MNIST batch-size experiment compares train and test accuracy at the same number of iterations, rather than holding epochs fixed. The plotted values are figure-only and the supplied text does not describe the direction or magnitude of the batch-size effect in words; thus no directional result row can be extracted. The proposed later-stage batch-size schedule is discussed theoretically, not tested.
No magnitude-aware sharpness measurement or comparison of generalization-gap predictors.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
